items.prose: A solver bisects a yield on $[0, 1]$ until the bracket is narrower than $10^{-8}$.
items.question: How many halvings does it need?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest $k$ with $2^k > 10^8$.

byKey.digits: You counted decimal places. Each halving divides by 2, not 10.
byKey.one-less: $2^{26} = 67{,}108{,}864$ is below $10^8$, so 26 halvings leave a bracket just wider than $10^{-8}$.

explain.text: After $k$ halvings the width is $2^{-k}$. $2^{26} \approx 6.7 \times 10^7$ is too small and $2^{27} \approx 1.34 \times 10^8$ is enough, so 27.

items.question: For which one does largest-coin-first fail for some amount?

options.why: Greedy is optimal for this system, as it is for UK coins. Try 6, 8 or 9: it is never beaten.
Powers of 3: greedy is optimal, as for any powers of one base.
This is the US system, for which greedy is optimal.

feedback.correct: For 15: greedy uses 12 + 1 + 1 + 1, but 5 + 5 + 5 is three coins.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try amounts just above the largest coin.

explain.text: Greedy takes 12 for 15 and is left with 3, which needs three 1s. Three 5s do it in three coins. A single counterexample settles it.

items.prose: Trades with equal prices must keep their arrival order after sorting by price.
items.question: Which sorts keep equal values in their original order? Select all that apply.

options.text: Merge sort, taking from the left half on a tie

options.why: Lomuto's swaps can jump a value past an equal one, as the final pivot swap does.
With `>=` a key walks past values equal to it, reversing their order.

feedback.correct: Insertion sort with `>`, merge sort with `<=`, and Timsort are stable.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each, ask whether an equal value can pass another.

explain.text: A sort is stable when equal values never pass each other. Shifting only on `>` and taking the left value on a tie ensure that. Lomuto swaps across long distances, so it is not stable.

items.prose: Quicksort with the last value as pivot runs on $n$ values already sorted. Let $C(n)$ be its comparisons.
items.question: Put the derivation in order.

lines.text: Partitioning $n$ values compares each non-pivot value once with the pivot: $n - 1$ comparisons
The pivot is the largest value, so the left side has $n - 1$ values and the right side none: $C(n) = (n - 1) + C(n - 1)$
So the worst case is $O(n^2)$, and the recursion is $n$ calls deep

feedback.correct: Each call peels off one value, so the costs form $1 + 2 + \dots + (n - 1)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with the cost of one partition.

explain.text: One lopsided split per level gives $n - 1$ levels with costs $n - 1, n - 2, \dots, 1$. Their sum is $n(n - 1)/2$. For 2,000 sorted prices that is 1,999,000 comparisons.

items.prose: A batch of orders must be processed in the given order over `days` days. Each day handles a run of consecutive orders whose sizes add up to at most the daily capacity. More capacity never needs more days.
items.question: Write `min_capacity(sizes, days)`: the smallest whole daily capacity that finishes within `days` days.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests: small batches, a single order, and 50,000 orders over 100 days. Two are extremes: one day per order (capacity is the largest order) and one day for all (the total).

feedback.correct: A search on the answer between the largest order and the total.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-6: Test 6 gives one day per order, so the capacity is the largest order, 10.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 has 50,000 orders. Trying every capacity in turn is too slow; bisect it.

explain.text: "Finishes within `days`" is False, then True, as capacity grows. A capacity below the largest order can never work, and the total always does. Bisecting that range costs $O(n \log(\text{total}))$.

items.prose: Twenty venues each send a sorted list of trade times. Merge them all into one sorted list. Merge the lists in pairs, then the results in pairs, as merge sort does. That costs $O(N \log k)$ for $N$ values in $k$ lists. `merge` is in the starter; do not call `sorted` or `.sort`.
items.question: Write `merge_k(lists)`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. They include three lists, no lists, empty lists, one list, mixed lengths with repeats, and 1,000 lists of 100. The last checks that you did not call `sorted`, `.sort` or `heapq`.

feedback.correct: Each round halves the number of lists, so each value is merged $\log_2 k$ times.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 passes no lists at all. Return `[]`.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 merges 1,000 lists. Merging each into one growing result is $O(Nk)$; merge in pairs.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 found `sorted`, `.sort` or `heapq` in your code. Use `merge` in rounds.

explain.text: Merging one list at a time into a growing result copies early values again and again: $O(Nk)$. Pairing lists, like the levels of merge sort, handles each value once per round, and there are $\lceil \log_2 k \rceil$ rounds.

items.prose: A desk wants the $k$th largest of a day's trade sizes ($k = 1$ is the largest) for several $k$. Use quickselect. Do not sort, do not use `heapq`, and leave the input list unchanged.
items.question: Write `kth_largest(xs, k)` in $O(n)$ average time.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. They ask for the largest, the 3rd and the smallest, and try one value, all equal values and repeats. Others check an unchanged input, 5,000 values already sorted and the 20,000th largest of 100,001 sizes. The last checks that you did not call `sorted`, `.sort` or `heapq`.

feedback.correct: The $k$th largest is index $n - k$ of the sorted order, found by quickselect on a copy.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 expects 7, the 3rd largest. Test 1 passed, so check how your target index depends on $k$: the $k$th largest sits at index `len(xs) - k` of the sorted order.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 checks the input is unchanged. Work on a copy, `a = list(xs)`.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 is 5,000 sorted values. A fixed first pivot drops one value per round, so a recursive version nests about 5,000 calls. That is past Python's recursion limit; pick the pivot at random.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 found `sorted`, `.sort` or `heapq` in your code. Use a partition instead.

explain.text: Translate to the smallest-first index `len(xs) - k`, copy the list, and run quickselect. Each round keeps one side, so the expected work is about $2n$ to $4n$. A random pivot keeps sorted input from being the worst case.

items.title: Designing a risk report
items.prompt:
Every hour a risk engine simulates 10 million P&L outcomes for a book. The report needs three things. (i) The 95% and 99% value at risk: the losses at the 5th and 1st percentiles. (ii) The median outcome. (iii) On request, how many outcomes lost more than an amount $L$. There are up to 500 such $L$ an hour.

(a) Compare a full sort with quickselect for (i) and (ii): cost in comparisons, extra memory, and worst case.
(b) Design the fastest way to answer (iii). Give its total cost.
(c) A colleague proposes quicksort with the first value as pivot, because the simulated outcomes arrive in random order. Say when this becomes dangerous and what you would use instead.
(d) Is stability needed anywhere here? Explain.
items.model:
**(a) Sort or select.** A full sort of $n = 10^7$ values costs about $n \log_2 n \approx 2.3 \times 10^8$ comparisons. Merge sort or Timsort is $O(n \log n)$ in every case and needs $O(n)$ extra memory. An in-place sort needs only $O(\log n)$ stack. Quickselect finds one order statistic in $O(n)$ on average, about $2n$ to $4n$, so $2$ to $4 \times 10^7$ comparisons. It works in place. Its worst case is $O(n^2)$: a random pivot makes that very unlikely, and median-of-medians rules it out.

We need three order statistics: indices $0.01n$, $0.05n$ and $0.5n$. Three quickselects cost about $6$ to $12 \times 10^7$ comparisons, still under a sort. Better: run quickselect for the median first, then the 5% index on the left part only. Then find the 1% index inside that. The ranges shrink, so the total is close to one quickselect.

**(b) Many thresholds.** For 500 values of $L$, sort once, $O(n \log n)$, then answer each with one bisection. The count of outcomes below $-L$ is `bisect_left(sorted_pnl, -L)`. Each costs about $\log_2 10^7 \approx 24$ comparisons, so 500 queries cost about 12,000: negligible. The sort dominates, at about $2.3 \times 10^8$. Running 500 linear scans would cost $5 \times 10^9$, twenty times more. Once the list is sorted, the percentiles in (a) are free lookups too. With (iii) in the report, a single sort is therefore the best plan.

**(c) First pivot.** Random input makes a first-value pivot fine on average. The danger is input that is not random: outcomes sorted by scenario, or a cached run that was already sorted. Then each partition peels off one value: $n(n-1)/2 \approx 5 \times 10^{13}$ comparisons and a recursion $10^7$ deep, which crashes Python. Use a random pivot or median-of-three, or simply the library sort (Timsort in Python, introsort in C++), which guarantees $O(n \log n)$.

**(d) Stability.** No. The report uses only values: percentiles and counts. Equal P&L values are interchangeable, so their order does not matter. Stability would matter if we sorted scenario records by P&L and read off the scenario behind each loss. Tied losses would then need a fixed order.

rubric.text: Costs a full sort (about $n \log_2 n \approx 2.3 \times 10^8$) and quickselect (about $2n$ to $4n$), with memory for each
States quickselect's $O(n^2)$ worst case and how a random pivot makes it unlikely
For (iii), sorts once and answers each threshold with a bisection, about 24 comparisons each
Compares the totals: one sort plus 500 bisections against 500 linear scans
Notes that once sorted, the percentiles are free lookups, so one sort serves the whole report
Explains when a first-value pivot turns quadratic (ordered input), and names a fix such as a random pivot
Says stability is not needed because only values are reported, and when it would matter

items.prose: A ring buffer holds a session's latest trades, one per slot. Trade sequence numbers rise through the session, and no two are the same. Once the buffer is full, each new trade overwrites the oldest slot. So `ring`, read from slot 0, is a sorted list turned at one point: in `[812, 815, 820, 803, 806, 809]` the oldest trade, 803, sits in slot 3. The buffer may not have turned yet, and it may be empty.
items.question: Write `find_trade(ring, seq)` with a binary search: the slot that holds sequence number `seq`, or `-1` if no slot does.

widget.how: Check runs 14 hidden tests. Test 12 searches a ring of 200,000 slots. Test 13 searches such a ring twice and counts the slots you read: at most 400. Test 14 calls a hidden `ring_sweep()`, which tries every turn of sorted lists of up to 12 numbers, for every number in them and every gap. It returns the number of wrong answers and the first one, as `[ring, seq, your answer]`.

feedback.correct: One side of `mid` is always in order, so each read still halves the slots left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 asks for 803 in `[812, 815, 820, 803, 806, 809]`, which is in slot 3. Return the slot in `ring` itself, not the place in sorted order.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 is an empty ring, so return `-1`. Check that a slot exists before you read one.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 is a ring that has not turned, `[3, 8, 9, 14]`, with 14 in the last slot. Your search must work with no turn at all.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 asks for 10 in `[3, 8, 9, 14]`, where it is absent. Check that the slot you end on holds `seq` before you return it.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 asks for 4 in `[9, 4]`. With two slots left, `lo` and `mid` are the same slot, and one slot is always in order: test it with `<=`, not `<`.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 asks for 9 in `[9, 4]`, which is in slot 0.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 is a single slot, `[7]`, searched for 7 and then for 6, so it expects `[0, -1]`.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 asks for 25, in the last slot of `[30, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25]`. When the slots from `mid` to `hi` are in order, the range check must include `ring[hi]`.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 asks for 20, in slot 0 of `[20, 25, 30, 5, 10, 15]`. A number equal to `ring[0]` or `ring[lo]` lies in the part before the turn, so include that end in the range check.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 asks for 4, 12, 22 and 31 in the same ring, where none of them is: one below every number, two in gaps and one above every number.
byKey.test-11: Test 11 turns at the last slot, `[5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 1]`, and asks for 1, 25 and 5.
byKey.test-12: Test 12 is a ring of 200,000 slots whose oldest trade sits in slot 62,983. It asks for slot 0, the last slot, the oldest and newest trades, one in the middle and three that are absent.
byKey.test-13: Test 13 searches a ring of 200,000 slots twice and counts every slot you read: at most 400 in all. Halving reads under 100 a search, so read single slots only, with no `in`, `index`, `min` or copy of the ring.
byKey.test-14: Test 14 found a ring where your answer is wrong, and shows the first as `[ring, seq, your answer]`. Run your function on that ring and follow `lo` and `hi` by hand.

explain.text: Whichever slot `mid` you read, the slots from `lo` to `mid` or those from `mid` to `hi` are in order, and that part's two ends say whether `seq` can lie in it. So each read still halves the slots left, and the search makes $O(\log n)$ reads. With two slots left `lo` equals `mid`, which is why the in-order test is `ring[lo] <= ring[mid]`.
